item.title: C/C++: How to Dynamically Increase Program Stack Size in C or GCC?
item.description:
“C/C++: How to Dynamically Increase Program Stack Size in C or GCC?”

When developing resource-intensive C or C++ applications, particularly those involving deep recursion or large local data structures, hitting the default stack size limit can result in a dreaded stack overflow. How can developers effectively manage and increase the available stack space either through code or compilation flags? We examine several accepted techniques for dynamically controlling the stack allocation.

item.title: GCC Auto-Vectorization Segfaults with Misaligned Pointers: Causes and Solutions
item.description:
“GCC Auto-Vectorization Segfaults with Misaligned Pointers: Causes and Solutions”

A common pitfall when leveraging compiler optimizations like auto-vectorization in C/C++ with GCC is the occurrence of segmentation faults (segfaults) when dealing with misaligned pointers. This issue typically surfaces when the compiler attempts to use SIMD instructions (like SSE2 on x86-64) to process data, but these instructions have strict alignment requirements.

The root cause often lies in how GCC’s auto-vectorizer makes assumptions about pointer alignment. For instance, when dealing with uint16_t* p, GCC might assume a 2-byte alignment for each element, enabling the use of movdqa instructions. However, if the pointer p points to a memory address that doesn’t conform to this alignment, movdqa can trigger a segfault because it requires aligned operands.

item.title: Why Does C Require -lm for Math Functions?
item.description:
“Why Does C Require -lm for Math Functions?”

Why Do C Programs Need the -lm Flag?

The necessity of the -lm flag stems from a combination of historical design choices, library organization, and compiler behavior. Let’s delve into the various perspectives that explain this requirement.

Historical Context and Library Design

Early C implementations, especially on resource-constrained systems, often separated the math library (libm) from the core C library (libc). This was partly due to the significant size and computational cost of floating-point operations on the hardware of the time. Not all programs utilized floating-point math, so excluding libm by default reduced executable sizes and potentially sped up compilation and linking.

item.title: GCC Regex Issues: When <regex> Fails and How to Fix It
item.description:
“GCC Regex Issues: When <regex> Fails and How to Fix It”

Encountering issues with the <regex> library in GCC, particularly in older versions, can be a significant hurdle for C++ developers. This exploration delves into why this might occur and presents practical approaches to circumvent these limitations.

The Root Cause: An Experimental Feature

The <regex> header in GCC was introduced as an experimental feature, initially implemented and released with GCC 4.9.0. Prior to this version, the implementation was not present, leading to compilation errors or unexpected behavior when developers attempted to use its functions. The early implementation was a work in progress, designed to align with early C++0x drafts. This approach allowed for developer feedback to influence the standardization process, a valuable aspect of open-source collaboration.
